tone_statements.quote: The major languages of the Burmish Family include Burmese, Achang, Xiandao, Maru, Atsi (Zaiwa), Bola, and Lashi, as indicated in the map in the top panel of Figure 2. As can be seen, four of the varieties were recorded in the same city (Máng City 芒市 in China, formerly called Lùxī 路西). When comparing the languages their close proximity must be borne in mind, as we should expect intensive language contact among them. Characteristics of the languages in this family include a generally isolating morphological structure, the use of lexical tone, and tense or creaky phonation.
tone_statements.locator: p. 56, section 4.1.1 'The Burmish language family'; data-source statement (Huáng et al. 1992 via STEDT) on p. 58, section 4.1.2

tone_statements.citation: Mann, Noel Walter. 1998. A phonological reconstruction of Proto Northern Burmic. MA thesis, University of Texas at Arlington.
tone_statements.quote: Bela has three tones in syllables with open and nasal codas. These tones are phonemically represented as a high falling /53/, a mid level tone /33/ and a falling-rising tone /323/. For notational simplicity, the falling-rising tone is represented as /23/ in this analysis. Stopped syllables have only one falling tone which may be realized as a high falling tone [53] or a relatively lower tone [42] depending on the voicing of the syllable and the initial consonant. Reduced syllables tend to assimilate to the tone of the following syllable.
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Tone system: three contrastive tones on open/nasal-coda syllables (/53/ high falling, /33/ mid level, /323/~/23/ falling-rising) plus one non-contrastive falling tone on stopped syllables ([53] or [42] by initial voicing). Domain: the syllable; 'Tone T is obligatory and maps over vocalic elements and the coda when it is occupied by a nasal' (sec. 2.2.2.2, p. 36). Tone sandhi: reduced syllables ass
